mission.title: Mission
mission.text: The Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB) is an independent center for the generation, use, and transfer of knowledge based on research and critical analysis of biomedical research. Our main goal is to provide data, trends, patterns, and diagnostics on the quality of methods, principles, and foresight of scientific activity.

ivan.title: CEO & Founder CECIMIB SAS (Colombia)
ivan.detailed_bio:
Ivan David Lozada-Martinez is a medical researcher and full-time professor at the Universidad de la Costa (Barranquilla, Colombia), where he conducts research at the intersection of meta-science, scientometrics, evidence-based research, knowledge gaps in medical sciences, evidence-based medicine, global health, and geroscience. Throughout his career, he has been characterized by addressing questions of high translational impact: how biomedical evidence is produced, evaluated, and improved, and how that knowledge can be converted into more precise decisions in clinical practice, policies, and health systems.

On an institutional and scientific leadership level, he is the Leader of the Biomedical Scientometrics and Evidence-Based Research Unit (METRIC-BIO) in his academic department, and also serves as Scientific Director of the CECIMIB research group (Center for Meta-Research and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences; Barranquilla), an initiative aimed at strengthening reproducible research, critical evaluation, and responsible metrics in health.

One of his most visible lines of work focuses on extreme longevity and healthy aging, with an emphasis on research on centenarians in Colombia. Within the context of the Colombia Centenarians Project/Alliance, he has contributed to characterizing centenarian populations and discussing their epidemiological and translational implications.

In parallel, his production includes contributions to international journals and forums where he poses scientific questions combining demographics, public health, and geroscience, such as the discussion on under-registration or missing centenarians as a problem with global implications, as well as work on the conceptualization of blue zones and their utility for guiding healthy aging research and policies.

Another cross-cutting line in his work is meta-research applied to biomedical sciences: evaluating methodological quality, bias, transparency, incentives, and knowledge gaps, with explicit calls to strengthen these approaches in specific areas (e.g., neurosciences), and to consolidate capacities in low- and middle-income contexts.

His scientific and academic agenda converges on one goal: to produce and use better evidence so that biomedical knowledge is more rigorous, useful, and equitable, connecting quantitative analysis of research (scientometrics/meta-science) with clinical and population problems (geroscience, public health, global health). His public projections are oriented towards expanding research platforms and initiatives, consolidating interdisciplinary collaborations, and continuing to develop projects that bring high-quality evidence closer to decision-making in health.

david.title: Research Assistant
david.detailed_bio: David A. Hernandez-Paez is a physician-in-training, associate researcher at the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences, and a member of the International Biometric Society. His academic activity focuses on meta-research and the assessment of scientific production coherence by estimating its potential impact on population indicators and health outcomes. His methodology utilizes regression models, hierarchical mixed-effects models, and moderator analysis. In 2025, he was awarded the Best Physician-in-Training Researcher in Colombia prize by the Association of Medical Student Scientific Societies of Colombia (ASCEMCOL).

andy.title: Research Assistant
andy.detailed_bio:
Andy A. Acosta-Monterrosa is a biologist from the University of Cartagena, research assistant at the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences, and member of the Colombian Association of Human Genetics and the Functional Diversity Research Network. His work integrates research in natural and biomedical sciences with a strong quantitative component, focusing on data management, analysis, and visualization, and biostatistics in R, in addition to scientific dissemination and communication.

His academic activity is organized into two axes; marine biodiversity of the Colombian Caribbean, with an emphasis on ecology, diversity and taxonomy of macroalgae, marine conservation and coastal governance; and bibliometrics and meta-research, studying scientific production, research coherence and global patterns in health and the environment.

Complementarily, he has developed research in pharmacogenomics and genetic ancestry in Colombian populations, exploring how differences in the frequency of genetic variants can be related to variation in response to medications and the implementation of precision medicine approaches.

1-1-2026.title: Congratulations to Dr. Fabriccio J. Visconti-Lopez on Achieving the Category of Distinguished Researcher RENACYT
1-1-2026.author: Andy A. Acosta-Monterrosa
1-1-2026.subtitle: Recognition of scientific excellence and rigor in Peru.
1-1-2026.p1: The Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB) expresses its congratulations to Dr. Fabriccio J. Visconti-Lopez, international collaborator and academic affiliated with our research group, for having achieved the category of Distinguished Researcher RENACYT, the highest classification granted by the National Council of Science, Technology and Technological Innovation, CONCYTEC, of Peru.
1-1-2026.p2: This recognition represents an important milestone in his career as a researcher and reflects his scientific production, academic commitment, methodological rigor, and contribution to the development of biomedical research, public health, and meta-research.
1-1-2026.p3: From CECIMIB, we highlight this achievement with special satisfaction, since approximately only 2% of the registered researchers in Peru obtain this distinction. This reaffirms the importance of promoting quality scientific research, with academic impact and oriented to answer relevant questions for health and society.
1-1-2026.p4: We commend Dr. Visconti-Lopez for this national recognition and express our gratitude to him for being part of our academic community. His trajectory constitutes an example of perseverance, discipline, and commitment to science.
1-1-2026.p5: Dr. Visconti-Lopez is an active contributor in the research lines of meta-science, evidence-based medicine, biomedical scientometrics, epidemiology, and global health.

1-2-2026.title: Recognition to Johana Patricia Galván Barrios: Top 10 Finalist of the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award 2026
1-2-2026.author: Andy A. Acosta-Monterrosa
1-2-2026.subtitle: A global achievement in nursing innovation and excellence.
1-2-2026.p1: From the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences, we express our most sincere recognition and congratulations to Johana Patricia Galván Barrios for having been selected among the Top 10 Finalists of the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award 2026, one of the most prestigious recognitions for nursing worldwide, organized by Aster DM Healthcare.
1-2-2026.p2: This important international achievement highlights her scientific trajectory, academic leadership, and commitment to the transformation of health systems through research, innovation, and emerging technologies applied to patient safety and quality of care. Her work in artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and 4.0 technologies reflects the impact that nursing can generate in strengthening public health and risk management in national and international contexts.
1-2-2026.p3: For CECIMIB, it is a matter of pride to have a professional whose trajectory represents excellence, discipline, and the generation of knowledge with social impact, contributing to the positioning of Latin American research in high-level global scenarios.
1-2-2026.p4: In our corporation, Johana Galván contributes to the lines of innovation and development in health, digital health, management of research and development projects, and public health.

1-4-2026.title: Does publishing more science mean improving people's lives?
1-4-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
1-4-2026.p1: Every year, millions of scientific articles are published worldwide. We are talking about new treatments, innovative technologies, artificial intelligence, vaccines, rare diseases, and hundreds of other topics. Science has never produced as much knowledge as it does now.
1-4-2026.p2: But there is a surprisingly simple question that for many years no one could clearly answer: Is all this research really helping to improve people's lives?
1-4-2026.p3: Although it may seem strange, the answer is not so obvious. For decades we have learned to measure how many articles a country publishes, how many times they are cited by other researchers, or in which journals they appear. These measurements are important because they allow us to understand scientific productivity. However, they all have one thing in common: they describe science from the inside.
1-4-2026.p4: What we rarely ask is whether this enormous scientific effort is truly aligned with the problems of society.
1-4-2026.p5: Imagine a city where more hospitals are built every year, but people continue to get sick from the same causes. No one would say that building hospitals is bad, but it would be reasonable to ask whether those hospitals are responding to the true needs of the population.
1-4-2026.p6: Something similar happens with scientific research. Publishing more does not guarantee, by itself, that diseases will decrease, treatments will improve, or public policies will be more effective. Precisely this was the question that motivated the approach of scientific coherence and development coherence.
1-4-2026.p7: Until now, there was no method specifically designed to study whether scientific production and health or development indicators evolved coherently over time. Most available tools evaluated the quality of publications, their academic impact, or the number of citations received, but very few analyzed the relationship between research and what happens in people's real lives.
1-4-2026.p8: To attempt to fill that gap, the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), developed a new methodological framework called DAIL, whose name comes from Data-driven Analysis and Inference of Longitudinal Population Indicators and Research Production.
1-4-2026.p9: Its purpose is not to say whether a research is good or bad. Its objective is much more ambitious; to estimate whether the growth of research on a topic seems to be accompanied by changes in indicators related to that same problem, and also to study how social, economic, or institutional conditions can influence a country's ability to produce science.
1-4-2026.p10: To understand it, an analogy may serve. Think of a doctor observing a patient's progress over several years. It is not enough to know how many medications the patient received; the doctor needs to compare that information with changes in blood pressure, weight, quality of life, and other indicators. Only then can they understand if there is a relationship between the treatment and the patient's progress.
1-4-2026.p11: DAIL applies a similar logic, but on a much larger scale. Instead of following a person, it analyzes countries, regions, or groups of countries over long periods. Instead of studying medications, it analyzes thousands of scientific publications. And instead of measuring only academic production, it compares it with health, development, education, or economic indicators available in international databases.
1-4-2026.p12: It is important to clarify something fundamental. This method does not demonstrate that research directly causes the observed changes. Reality is much more complex. The results allow identifying patterns of association and coherence, but always recognizing that there are many other factors that also influence and that causality cannot be established with this type of analysis. This methodological prudence is an essential part of the method itself.
1-4-2026.p13: Why does this matter for society, academia, and decision-making in research policies? If we learn to measure how aligned research is with the needs of the population, we can identify areas where science is generating a positive impact, but also those where there is an enormous research effort without yet reflecting benefits for society. This information can help guide future research, support decision-making, and strengthen evidence-based scientific policies.
1-4-2026.p14: Science has always sought to answer questions about the phenomena of nature. However, perhaps the time has come to ask a different question: how well is science itself responding to people's needs?
1-4-2026.p15: Answering that question does not only imply producing more knowledge. It implies learning to evaluate whether that knowledge advances coherently with the health, well-being, and development of societies. That was the reason that drove the construction of the DAIL method and, probably, one of the tools that seeks to contribute to the relevance and pertinence of scientific and academic activity in the 21st century.
1-4-2026.reference: Hernandez-Paez DA, Visconti-Lopez FJ, Lozada-Martınez ID. Estimating scientific coherence using population-level indicators and research production data: a longitudinal analytical proof-of-concept study. Front Res Metr Anal. 2026 Jun 29;11:1817595.
1-4-2026.caption: Scientific coherence study published in Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics for global development.

1-5-2026.title: Does researching a disease guarantee that it stops affecting people?
1-5-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
1-5-2026.p1: Every year, millions of people get sick from causes that most of the world never mentions. They do not frequently appear on the news, they rarely occupy the front pages of newspapers, and for many people, even their names are unknown. These are the so-called neglected tropical diseases.
1-5-2026.p2: Despite affecting more than a billion people, these diseases tend to concentrate in communities with high levels of poverty, limited access to health services, and few development opportunities. Over the past decades, the scientific community has devoted increasing efforts to studying them. Thousands of articles have been published, new projects developed, and international collaborations strengthened. But a question arose that seemed as simple as it was uncomfortable:
1-5-2026.p3: Is all this research really reaching those who need it most?
1-5-2026.p4: Answering that question was the purpose of a recently published study. To do so, the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), developed a study that included more than 107,000 research articles published over 25 years and compared them with international health indicators, such as the incidence of malaria, tuberculosis, HIV, and other neglected tropical diseases in different regions of the world.
1-5-2026.p5: This analysis did not seek to prove that research directly caused an improvement in health, because reality is much more complex. It aimed to explore whether both seemed to advance in the same direction, that is, if there was coherence between the knowledge that science produces and what happens to the health of populations.
1-5-2026.p6: The results were encouraging, but they also left important lessons. It was identified that, in several cases, a higher volume of research was associated with reductions in indicators related to HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, and some tropical diseases. However, this relationship did not appear in all indicators nor in all regions of the world. In some places, research seemed to advance much faster than the benefits observed in the population.
1-5-2026.p7: Why does this happen? Because publishing a scientific article is just the beginning of the road.
1-5-2026.p8: For a discovery to change a person's life, it must be transformed into public policies, prevention programs, available medications, trained professionals, and health systems capable of bringing that knowledge to communities. If any of those steps fail, even the best research can take many years to produce real benefits.
1-5-2026.p9: We can imagine it as a relay race. The researcher passes the baton to those who design health policies, then to those who organize health services, and finally to the professionals who care for patients. If any of those batons are dropped, knowledge never reaches the finish line. That was probably the most important lesson from our study.
1-5-2026.p10: It is not enough to produce more science. We must also ask whether that science is responding to people's needs and whether the conditions exist to turn knowledge into concrete actions. Research should not be evaluated solely by the number of articles published, but also by its capacity to contribute to solving the problems it attempts to study.
1-5-2026.p11: Neglected tropical diseases are named so because, for a long time, they were also neglected by research, funding, and public policies. Today we know that scientific production is growing and that this growth is already beginning to be reflected in some health indicators. However, this research shows that there is still a long way to go for this knowledge to equitably benefit all populations.
1-5-2026.p12: The true success of science is not measured solely by the articles it publishes, but by the lives it manages to transform.
1-5-2026.reference: Hernandez-Paez DA, Montoya-Quintero KF, Vidal-Durango JV, Lozada-Martínez ID. Measuring scientific coherence between global neglected tropical disease research and population health indicators: a 25-year meta-research study. Front Res Metr Anal. 2026 Jun 18;11:1766718.
1-5-2026.caption: Scientific coherence study published in Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics for tropical diseases.

1-6-2026.title: Can research on neglected tropical diseases transform more than just health?
1-6-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
1-6-2026.p1: When we think of research on neglected tropical diseases, it is common to imagine new medications, vaccines, or diagnostic tests. However, these diseases do not depend solely on medical advances. They are also closely related to access to clean water, sanitation, hygiene, the strength of health systems, and the ability of countries to generate their own scientific knowledge.
1-6-2026.p2: This raises a rare but fundamental question: can scientific research on neglected tropical diseases contribute to transforming these conditions, in addition to improving health?
1-6-2026.p3: Based on this question, the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), analyzed more than one hundred thousand research articles published over the past two decades and linked them with international indicators on access to health services, research investment, clean water, sanitation, and hygiene. Furthermore, they compared the results among high, middle, and low-income countries to understand whether the potential benefits of research were similar in different socioeconomic contexts.
1-6-2026.p4: The results showed a complex reality. In general terms, the researchers found that scientific activity does seem to be associated with improvements in some key indicators, but those benefits are not evenly distributed. That is, producing more knowledge does not guarantee that all countries obtain the same advantages.
1-6-2026.p5: The most consistent findings appeared in indicators related to water, sanitation, and hygiene, internationally known as WASH. It was observed that a higher volume of research was associated with a decrease in open defecation practices and a reduction in deaths related to unsafe sanitary conditions. Most interestingly, these associations were more pronounced in low-income countries, precisely where neglected tropical diseases represent a greater burden on the population.
1-6-2026.p6: They also identified positive associations with greater access to safely managed drinking water and, in some groups of countries, with better handwashing facilities. This suggests that research can contribute, indirectly, to strengthening essential environmental conditions to prevent the transmission of many of these diseases.
1-6-2026.p7: However, not all areas showed the same behavior. When scientific capacity and technological development were analyzed, important differences were found among country groups. In high-income nations, a greater availability of health research institutions was related to an increase in scientific production. Conversely, in several middle and low-income countries, that relationship was much more limited or even negative. Likewise, funding specifically destined for research on neglected tropical diseases produced different effects depending on each country's income level, demonstrating that investing resources does not always generate the same results in all contexts.
1-6-2026.p8: Results related to the state of health systems were also discovered. Scientific activity was associated with a reduction in out-of-pocket spending for accessing health services, especially in low and lower-middle-income countries. This finding suggests that scientific knowledge could contribute to more efficient health systems when conditions exist to incorporate evidence into decision-making.
1-6-2026.p9: Perhaps the most important lesson from this study is that research does not act only within hospitals or laboratories. Its effects can extend to much broader aspects, such as sanitation conditions, access to safe water, the organization of health systems, or a country's ability to generate innovation.
1-6-2026.p10: Neglected tropical diseases are, in essence, diseases deeply linked to social inequalities. Therefore, fighting them requires much more than developing new treatments. It also requires strengthening the conditions that allow preventing them, controlling them, and generating solutions from their own territories. Scientific research can be an engine of that change, but only when it is accompanied by public policies, sustained investment, and a real commitment to equity.
1-6-2026.reference: Hernandez-Paez DA, Lozada-Martinez ID, Reyes-Duque JD, Kalokoh S. Estimating the potential impact of global research on neglected tropical diseases on population-level indicators of health access, sanitation, and research capacity. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2026 May 21;20(5):e0014343.
1-6-2026.caption: Research impact study published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases for sanitation indicators.
